title: Lists and Generics
lede: Replace fixed-size arrays with collections, compare ArrayList and LinkedList, distinguish positions from values, and use type parameters to reuse code without giving up type checking.

sections.title: ArrayList and Python lists
concepts: An array has a fixed length. An ArrayList manages a backing array and its capacity for you, so adding an element does not require you to allocate a replacement yourself. size() is the number of stored elements; capacity is internal storage, not a set of elements you can already access.

Use add(value) to append, add(index,value) to insert and set(index,value) to replace. Valid access indices run from 0 through size−1. Insertion also permits size, which appends. Python uses append, insert and bracket assignment for the corresponding jobs.

visuals.title: Room to grow: size versus capacity
visuals.intro: How can a list grow when an array cannot? This small GrowList does what ArrayList does inside: it keeps an ordinary array with some spare slots, and when the array is full it makes a bigger one and copies everything across. Press Next and watch size (the elements) and the capacity (the slots).

programs.code:
class GrowList:
    def __init__(self):
        self.items = [None] * 4
        self.size = 0

    def add(self, value):
        if self.size == len(self.items):
            bigger = [None] * (len(self.items) + len(self.items) // 2)
            for i in range(self.size):
                bigger[i] = self.items[i]
            self.items = bigger
        self.items[self.size] = value
        self.size += 1

    def get(self, index):
        if index >= self.size:
            raise IndexError("index " + str(index) + ", size " + str(self.size))
        return self.items[index]


names = GrowList()
names.add("An")
names.add("Mai")
names.add("Tuan")
names.add("Linh")
names.add("Binh")
print(names.size, "of", len(names.items))
print(names.get(4))

names = []

names.append("Mai")
names.append("Tuan")

steps.say: An empty list. Its size is 0, so there is no valid index yet.
An goes on the end, at index 0. The size is now 1.
Mai goes on the end, at index 1. The list grows by itself: no fixed length, unlike an array.
Tuan goes on the end, at index 2. The size is 3, so the valid indexes are 0, 1 and 2.
Linh goes into index 1. Mai and Tuan each move one place right, so their indexes go up by 1. The size is 4.
set replaces the value at index 0: An is gone and Binh takes its place. Nothing moves and the size stays 4.
Remove index 2. Mai comes out and is stored in gone. Tuan moves left into index 2. The size is 3.
Print the value that was removed. Both languages give it back to you.
The same list, printed two ways: Java shows [Binh, Linh, Tuan], Python shows the quotes, ['Binh', 'Linh', 'Tuan'].
get(1) in Java, names[1] in Python: read index 1 without changing anything.

media.alt: A clear plastic carton for 24 eggs lying open on a wooden floor, holding 21 brown eggs with three empty cups at the front
media.caption: This carton has cups for 24 eggs but holds 21. The cups are the capacity: storage the ArrayList has set aside. The eggs are the size(): the elements actually in the list, at indexes 0 to 20 — an empty cup is not an element, so get(21) fails even though there is room. When a 25th egg arrives, ArrayList fetches a bigger carton and moves every egg across for you; with a plain array you would have to do that yourself.

media.alt: A tightly packed shelf of hardback books of different heights and colours, editions of Aristotle's Metaphysics and Physics
media.lead: Make room, and everything to the right moves.
media.caption: Push a new book in between two others and every book to its right slides along one place. That is add(i, x): the new element takes index i and every later element's index goes up by one. Swapping one book for another moves nothing else — that is set(i, x). You can only take down a book that is there (positions 0 to size()−1), but you may add one at position size(), the very end. Where it breaks: you shove a row of books in one push, but the list moves each element separately, so inserting near the front of a long list is real work.

media.title: Donald Knuth
media.alt: xkcd comic: one programmer tells another he is being inconsistent with his array indices, some starting from one and some from zero. The other replies that different tasks call for different conventions, and quotes algorithms expert Donald Knuth as saying “Who are you? How did you get in my house?” — which is what Knuth said when he asked him about it.
media.caption: Java and Python both count from 0, so the last index is the size minus 1. Mixing 0 and 1 is how off-by-one bugs start.

media.alt: A red hermit crab walking on sand, carrying a large striped snail shell as its home
media.text: A real ArrayList grows just like the GrowList above. In OpenJDK's source code, when the backing array is full, grow() makes a new array about 1.5 times as big (the old capacity plus oldCapacity >> 1, which is half of it) and copies every element across, like a hermit crab moving into a bigger shell. A new ArrayList<>() gets room for 10 elements the first time you add. The official Javadoc promises only that add has "constant amortized time cost", so this exact rule belongs to the implementation, not the specification.

sections.title: Removal and safe traversal
concepts: On ArrayList<Integer>, remove(1) removes index 1; remove(Integer.valueOf(1)) removes the first value equal to 1. The argument type decides the overload. A value removal that finds no match returns false; a position outside the list is an error.
Do not shift the ground under your loop

Removing from a list while an enhanced for-loop is traversing it can invalidate the traversal. Use an Iterator and its remove method, iterate indices backwards, or create a filtered result. The Python example creates a new list, so repeated adjacent rejected values are handled correctly.

visuals.title: Removing while you loop: find the skipped value
visuals.intro: The goal is to remove every even number from [1, 2, 2, 3, 4]. Pick a version, then step through it. The arrow above the boxes is the loop variable, and the highlighted line is the one that has just run.

strategies.label: Forward loop (bug)

python.code:
values = [1, 2, 2, 3, 4]
i = 0
while i < len(values):
    if values[i] % 2 == 0:
        values.pop(i)
    i += 1
print(values)

strategies.end: The output is [1, 2, 3]: one 2 survived. After each removal the next value slides into the index the loop has just checked, and the next step of i jumps past it. Python's for v in values: with values.remove(v) skips values in exactly the same way.

strategies.label: Backwards loop (fix)
strategies.end: The output is [1, 3]. Removing at i only moves the values to the right of i, and the loop has already checked those. Nothing is skipped.

strategies.label: Build a new list (fix)
strategies.end: The output is [1, 3]. The original list never changes while the loop reads it, so nothing can shift. This is also what the list comprehension below does.

media.alt: Rows of light-blue stadium seats, each with a number painted on it; the second row from the front reads 219, 217, 215, 213, 211, 209
media.caption: Every seat here has two numbers: its position in the row, counted from 0 at the left, and the number painted on it. In the second row from the front (219, 217, 215, 213…), position 1 holds the seat painted 217. On an ArrayList<Integer>, remove(1) means “the seat at position 1”, while remove(Integer.valueOf(211)) means “the seat with 211 painted on it”, wherever it is. Java chooses between them from the argument's type: a plain int is a position, an Integer is a value.

media.alt: Numbered folding stadium seats in white, yellow, blue and red; in the front row seats 21 and 22 are both yellow, between a white 20 and a blue 23
media.lead: Remove 21, and 22 slides into the place you just checked.
media.caption: Walk along the front row removing every yellow seat, with everything to its right sliding one place left to close the gap (real seats are bolted down; a list's elements are not). At 21 you find yellow and remove it, so yellow 22 slides into the place you have just checked; you step on and find 23, and 22 is never looked at. That is what removing inside a forward loop over indexes does to two neighbouring matches. Walk from the right-hand end instead, let an Iterator do the removing, or copy the seats you keep into a new list.

sections.title: Linked nodes and queues
concepts: Follow links instead of shifting values

A linked list stores nodes with links between them. Java LinkedList is doubly linked. Adding or removing at an end does not shift a backing array, but reaching the node at an arbitrary index still requires traversal. A fast unlink after finding a node does not make every remove(index) constant time.

ArrayList is a sound default for indexed access and ordinary traversal. LinkedList offers operations at both ends. Repeated get(i) in a loop can make a linked-list traversal quadratic; an enhanced for-loop visits it sequentially. For a Python FIFO queue, collections.deque avoids repeatedly shifting the front of a list.

The front of the queue: the next node to leave.
The back of the queue. Keeping it means enqueue never has to walk along the whole chain.

media.alt: A handwritten treasure-hunt note propped beside a wrapped sweet, reading “A lantern named Jack will light the way to clue #3!”, with a glowing jack-o'-lantern blurred in front
media.lead: A value, and the way to the next one.
media.caption: Each clue in a treasure hunt holds a small prize and says where the next clue is — this one leads to clue #3. That is a linked-list node: one value plus a link to the next node, and the nodes can sit anywhere. To reach clue 5 you cannot jump there; you start at the first clue and follow every link, which is why reaching index i in a LinkedList means walking. Once you are standing at the right clue, adding a new one only means rewriting one note — nothing else has to shift. Where it breaks: Java's LinkedList nodes also point back to the previous node, so it can be walked from either end.

media.alt: A line of people waiting inside a chain barrier to board a shuttle bus at Grand Canyon; an ENTER HERE sign marks the back of the line
media.caption: People join at the back, where the sign says ENTER HERE, and board at the front, so whoever has waited longest gets on first: first in, first out. A queue only ever uses its two ends, which is why a LinkedList or Python's collections.deque suits it. Taking the first element out of an ArrayList or Python list is like making everyone in this line step forward one place each time the bus takes a passenger. Where it breaks: in a real line people do step forward; in a deque or linked list nothing moves — only the record of who is at the front changes.

media.title: Linked List Interview Problem
media.alt: xkcd comic: at a coding interview, asked to traverse a linked list, a candidate writes a function on the whiteboard that emails the list’s head pointer to a technology museum as an item donation. The interviewer says “Hey.” Caption: Coding interview tip: interviewers get really mad when you try to donate their linked lists to a technology museum.
media.caption: A linked list is reached only through its head. Hand that one reference away and the whole list goes with it.

media.alt: The JOHNNIAC computer: a wall of tall cabinets packed with vacuum tubes and wiring, with its control consoles in front
media.text: Linked lists go back to 1956, when Allen Newell, Cliff Shaw and Herbert Simon described IPL, a list-processing language for the RAND Corporation's JOHNNIAC computer, built for their Logic Theorist program. In IPL each list was a chain of "location words": one address pointed at the item, the other at the next location word, and a negative number ended the list. To delete B from the list A, B, C they simply changed A's link to point at C, the same relinking trick Java's LinkedList uses in remove.
sources: Newell & Shaw, “Programming the Logic Theory Machine”, RAND P-954 (1957), scan

sections.title: Type parameters and programming to List
concepts: Box<T> describes one class parameterised by a reference type. Box<String> accepts strings and returns a String. A raw Box would discard useful checking. Primitive types cannot be type arguments: use Integer rather than int. Boxing and unboxing bridge the two, but unboxing a null Integer fails.

A method accepting List<Integer> can work with ArrayList or LinkedList when it needs only the List operations. Neither List<Integer> nor List<Double> is a subtype of List<Number>. Generic type arguments are invariant. This page introduces the idea; wildcard bounds and type erasure are further reading.

media.alt: A row of identical amber glass apothecary jars with stoppers on a glass shelf, each with an ornate paper label naming a different chemical
media.lead: The same jar; the label says what goes in.
media.caption: Every jar on this shelf is made to the same design; only the label changes. Box<T> is the design and the type argument is the label: Box<String>, ArrayList<Book>. Because the label is part of the type, the compiler refuses to put the wrong thing in, and you know exactly what comes out without checking. Where it breaks: a paper label cannot stop anyone pouring in the wrong powder, but the compiler does stop you — and the label must name a class, so it is Integer, not int.

media.alt: A white Australian double power point on a wall, with two switches and two three-pin sockets
media.lead: Any plug of the standard shape fits.
media.caption: This power point does not care whether a kettle, a lamp or a phone charger is plugged in, as long as the plug has the standard shape. A method whose parameter is List<Integer> is the socket: an ArrayList or a LinkedList both fit, because the method uses only the operations every List promises. One thing does not follow: a List<Integer> is not a List<Number>. If it were, code holding it as a list of Numbers could add a Double to it — like pouring rice into the sugar jar because both are “food”.

media.title: Workflow
media.alt: xkcd comic: a software changelog for version 10.17 reads “The CPU no longer overheats when you hold down spacebar.” A long-time user complains the update broke his workflow, because he holds spacebar instead of the hard-to-reach Control key and configured his editor to treat the rapid temperature rise as Control. The admin replies “That’s horrifying.” Caption: Every change breaks someone’s workflow.
media.caption: He relied on behaviour nobody promised. Code that uses only what List promises keeps working when the implementation changes.

media.alt: A Bengal tiger walking through long grass in front of green bushes
media.text: Java only got generics in J2SE 5.0, code-named "Tiger", finalised in September 2004 through JSR 14, "Add Generic Types to the Java Programming Language", a request first approved back in 1999. Before that a collection held plain Objects, so every get needed a cast like (String) list.get(0), and a wrong cast only failed when the program ran. The release notes said generics "eliminates the drudgery of casting": now the compiler checks your ArrayList<String> for you.

questions.q: Which declaration uses an allowed element type?
wrong: ArrayList<int> values = new ArrayList<int>(); // use primitive int directly
ArrayList<double> values = new ArrayList<double>(); // primitive doubles
ArrayList<boolean> values = new ArrayList<boolean>(); // primitive booleans
questions.why: Generic arguments are reference types; wrapper classes represent primitives.

questions.q: Why can remove(index) on LinkedList take linear time?
questions.correct: Finding the node at that index may require traversal.
wrong: Every linked-list removal must shift all later values into adjacent array slots.
Java always copies the whole list into an ArrayList before removing a single node.
Every linked-list node is sorted numerically whenever an index is supplied.
questions.why: Relinking is cheap once positioned, but an index is not a direct node reference.

questions.q: A list has size 3. Which index is valid for add(index,value) but not get(index)?
wrong: 2, because a list of size 3 has no element at any even numbered index.
1, because insertion positions and element indices always have opposite parity.
0, because inserting before the first item makes index zero inaccessible.
questions.why: Insertion at size appends; element access requires an existing element.

questions.q: Why should total accept List<Integer> instead of ArrayList<Integer>?
questions.correct: It needs iteration, not one particular storage implementation.
wrong: It makes every implementation automatically use exactly the same amount of memory.
It forces LinkedList to store its elements in a contiguous backing array.
It disables compile-time type checking so mixed element types can be accepted freely.
questions.why: Using the required abstraction admits multiple implementations without requiring irrelevant details.

exercises.title: Remove duplicates in Java
exercises.brief: Read n, then n integers on the next line (possibly empty when n is 0). Print the values with duplicates removed, preserving first occurrence, separated by single spaces. Print an empty line for an empty result.

exercises.title: Remove duplicates in Python
exercises.brief: Read n, then n integers on the next line (possibly empty when n is 0). Print the values with duplicates removed, preserving first occurrence, separated by single spaces. Print an empty line for an empty result.
exercises.starter:
n=int(input())
values=list(map(int,input().split()))
# preserve the first occurrence of each value

exercises.title: Delete one occurrence by value
exercises.brief: Read n, then n integers, then a target integer. Remove only its first occurrence by value and print the remaining list using Java list formatting.

exercises.title: A waiting queue
exercises.brief: Read n names, one per line, then k (0 ≤ k ≤ n). Serve and print the first k names in arrival order. Finally print Waiting: N for the number left. Use deque.
exercises.starter:
from collections import deque
n=int(input())
# read names and serve k people
exercises.solution:
from collections import deque
n=int(input())
queue=deque(input() for _ in range(n))
k=int(input())
for _ in range(k): print(queue.popleft())
print(f"Waiting: {len(queue)}")

exercises.title: One typed pair
exercises.brief: Read a name on one line and an integer on the next. Implement Pair<A,B> with a constructor and two getters; store the input in Pair<String,Integer>. Print name: number.

exercises.title: Keep passing marks
exercises.brief: Read one line of integer marks, possibly empty. Print only marks ≥ 50 in their original order, separated by single spaces; use an empty line if none pass.
exercises.starter:
marks=list(map(int,input().split()))
# build a filtered list and print it
exercises.solution:
marks=list(map(int,input().split()))
passed=[mark for mark in marks if mark>=50]
print(*passed)
